_meta.title: Observation places, historical and modern names with coordinates
_meta.scope: The recurring capitals and observing places named in the record corpus: the successive Chinese capitals, ancient western observing sites such as Babylon, Nineveh and Alexandria, and the modern East Asian observatories. Each entry gives one set of coordinates together with the historical name, its romanisation and the modern name. Places mentioned once in passing are not collected here; their names stay with the record that mentions them.
_meta.fields: key = place identifier. name = historical name in zh-Hans, zh-Hant, en, fr, es, it, ja, given as a bare settlement name; en is the Latin-script form, which for Chinese places is the romanisation and elsewhere the common English name, and fr/es/it/ja appear only where they differ from en. modern = present-day name, same language keys, zh-Hans always present and the rest only where they differ from it (optional). A language in which the place was never renamed still states the name here rather than omitting the key: an omitted key sends the display ladder on to the next language, which for Chinese ends at English and would put Latin script inside a Chinese label. The display side drops a modern name that resolves to the historical one, so restating it costs nothing and omitting it is what breaks. aliases = historical variant names, an array per language (optional). since/until = the years between which the entry applies, in astronomical years, since inclusive and until exclusive (optional). lat/lon = position in decimal degrees.
_meta.provenance: Coordinates and Chinese historical names are drawn from the gazetteer that underlies the corpus; coordinates themselves are not subject to copyright, and the historical atlases consulted while building it are not redistributed here. Names in the other languages and all modern names are established by hand rather than transliterated mechanically, so that Constantinople maps to Istanbul.
